entities.name: Clara Tott
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Clara Tott (c. 1440, Augsburg – 1520), also known by variants such as Clara Dett, Clara of Dettingen, or Clare Dettin, was a distinguished court singer whose life became inextricably linked with the complex dynastic politics of the Holy Roman Empire through her alleged secret marriage to Frederick I, the Elector Palatine. Her story, a blend of artistic talent and political intrigue, illuminates the social mobility possible for women of exceptional skill within the princely courts of the late Medieval and early Renaissance periods, even as it highlights the rigid class distinctions and succession laws that governed European nobility. Her existence posed a significant challenge to the established order of the House of Wittelsbach, making her a figure of enduring historical interest for understanding power, gender, and legitimacy in 15th-century Germany.

Born in Augsburg around 1440, Clara Tott rose to prominence as a captivating singer at the Palatine court in Heidelberg. Her relationship with Frederick I, a powerful prince-elector who ruled the Palatinate from 1451 to 1476, began sometime in the 1460s. Historical sources suggest a secret, morganatic marriage took place between them around 1471, a union that was never officially recognized by the Imperial Diet or the Wittelsbach family due to her commoner status. From this union, two sons were born: Frederick (1471–1517) and Louis (1473–1523), both of whom were later ennobled as Counts of Löwenstein, establishing a new cadet branch of the Wittelsbach dynasty.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Clara Tott's life significantly impacted the succession of the Electoral Palatinate by challenging dynastic norms and directly leading to the establishment of the Löwenstein cadet branch of the Wittelsbach family, whose descendants remain relevant in German aristocracy.
